title: Representative stable isotopes: Coulomb ratio and Diophantine error
html:
Remark. Representative stable isotopes: Coulomb ratio and Diophantine error

Table: Representative stable isotopes shows representative elements spanning the periodic table. It compares the continuous beta-stability prediction p^*(A) (beta-stability) with the observed stable proton number, the neutron-to-proton ratio, and the Diophantine error \varepsilon = |p_{\mathrm{stab}} - p^*|.

Observations.

  1. Light nuclei (A \leq 40). The ratio n/p \approx 1. The Coulomb correction c \cdot A^{2/3} is small. The curve coincides with the diagonal p = A/2.
  2. Medium nuclei (40 < A \leq 120). The ratio n/p rises from 1.0 to 1.4. The Coulomb term bends the curve below the diagonal, requiring extra neutrons.
  3. Heavy nuclei (A > 120). The ratio n/p \to 1.6. The p^2 growth of the Coulomb penalty dominates. The curve flattens.
  4. Stability pairs (\diamond, \star). Helium, calcium, tin, and lead have anomalously low Diophantine error and closed Skein shell structure. The doubly-magic stable nuclei (^4He, ^{40}Ca, ^{208}Pb) combine \varepsilon < 0.8 with shell closure.
  5. Iron peak. The maximum binding energy per nucleon B/A \approx 8.79 MeV occurs at ^{56}Fe. Here the competition between volume binding (\propto A) and Coulomb repulsion (\propto p^2/A^{1/3}) is optimally balanced.

The continuous curve p^*(A) and the integer lattice points (p_{\mathrm{stab}}, n_{\mathrm{stab}}) are illustrated in the valley of stability simulator.
